events.description: al-Qaeda US embassy bombings, after which Hassan Akhund made statements
Hassan Akhund says the Taliban will not turn over bin Laden after UN sanctions threat
UN sanctions four of the five future Guantanamo swap detainees (January or February 2001)
al-Qaeda kills Ahmad Shah Massoud; Fazl then coordinates with Abdul Hadi al-Iraqi on an offensive against the Northern Alliance
Khairkhwa brokers a deal with the Iranian government to work together against America after the invasion (late 2001)
al-Qaeda ransom exchange for an Afghan ambassador yields $5 million; Ibrahim Haqqani identified as key guarantor/mediator
Five Guantanamo detainees exchanged for Bowe Bergdahl, held by the Haqqanis
Taliban video saying the US deserved 9/11, released during talks with the Trump administration
Doha agreement signed between the Trump administration and the Taliban
Mark Esper fired as Secretary of Defense
Abdul Haq, son of Mohammad Nabi Omari, killed in fighting in Khost and celebrated by the Taliban
Dr. Amin al-Haq escorted by the Taliban in a military convoy to his home in Nangarhar
Taliban air the third 'Victorious Force' installment on RTA, gloating over 9/11 and blaming America

New Taliban cabinet named with Hassan Akhund as head of state, Sirajuddin Haqqani as interior minister, Khalil Haqqani as refugees minister, Wasiq as intelligence director, Noori and Fazl in senior roles, Nabi Omari as Khost governor
Amid UN sanctions threats, Hassan Akhund said the Taliban would not turn over bin Laden at any price.
Mullah Omar defiantly refused to turn over bin Laden, calling it a matter of Islam's prestige.
9/11 attacks killing about 3,000 Americans; hosts recorded the episode on September 10, 2021.
Hassan Akhund became head of state of the Taliban's regime, a promotion from his previous foreign minister post.
A Taliban spokesman recently said there was no evidence that bin Laden or al-Qaeda was responsible for 9/11.

key_claims: The Taliban uses the Doha agreement to argue the US cannot target Sirajuddin Haqqani, Khalil Haqqani or other leaders.
The Haqqani Network is an integral part of the Taliban and al-Qaeda's closest ally, so US claims that the two are separate are ignorance or lies.
The new Taliban cabinet is largely the old 1996-2001 regime; 17 of 33 ministers were UN-sanctioned, mostly before 9/11.
Five ex-Guantanamo detainees swapped for Bergdahl in 2014 now hold senior posts, and all had al-Qaeda ties before 9/11.
The Taliban were defeated on the battlefield in 2001-02 but never strategically defeated because their senior and religious leaders survived.
The Taliban's 2021 cabinet is full of old personalities, such as Hassan Akhund, who is now head of state.
Hassan Akhund defended refusing to hand over bin Laden in 1999 and held several posts in the first regime.
The Taliban remain al-Qaeda's closest ally, and claims that they were willing to negotiate over bin Laden in 2001 are false.
The Taliban still claim there is no evidence that bin Laden or al-Qaeda was responsible for 9/11.
Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State share the same goals and operate in more regions, so the US war on terror was a strategic failure despite tactical wins.
